name: Hydroxyprogesterone caproate

card.summary: A long-acting injectable progestin used in hormone-related care, from gynecology to feminizing hormone therapy, where progestogens are part of how some people shape their body's hormonal profile.
card.note: Prescription drug; its US approval for preterm birth was withdrawn in 2023.

quick.overview:
Hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) is a synthetic progestogen delivered as an oil-based intramuscular injection that releases slowly over days. It was developed at Schering in the 1950s and has been used in gynecology, in some hormone therapies and, most prominently, to try to reduce repeat preterm birth.

For appearance-minded readers, its relevance is through hormone therapy: it is listed as a component of menopausal and feminizing hormone regimens and of some combined injectable contraceptives, where progestogens sit alongside estrogens.
quick.mechanism: It is a progesterone derivative with a caproate ester on the 17-hydroxy group. The ester makes it fat-soluble so it depots in muscle and is released gradually. It acts on progesterone receptors; reported half-life is about a week in non-pregnant women and longer in pregnancy.
quick.risks: Injection-site pain and swelling are the most commonly reported effects. The US label for the non-pregnant-indication product lists thromboembolic events, vision-related warnings, glucose tolerance changes and allergic reactions. The FDA withdrew approval of Makena in April 2023 after the PROLONG trial; the drug is prescription-only.

chain: Acts on progesterone receptors for days to weeks
Used within some menopausal, feminizing and gynecologic hormone regimens
angle.text: Hydroxyprogesterone caproate is a depot progestogen. It appears as a component of some hormone therapies, including feminizing therapy for transgender women and combined injectable contraceptives, where hormone balance influences body and skin changes people seek. It is a prescription medicine managed by clinicians.

lead: Hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) is a synthetic progestogen, an ester of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, given by intramuscular injection so that it releases slowly [1][2]. Karl Junkmann developed it at Schering AG in 1953, and it was marketed in the US as Delalutin from 1956 [2].

In the context of appearance and body goals, it is relevant as one of the progestogens used in hormone therapy: it is described as part of menopausal and feminizing hormone therapy and of combined monthly injectable contraceptives in some countries [2]. Its best-known use, however, has been in obstetrics, to lower the risk of repeat preterm birth.

Research is extensive for that obstetric use. A 2003 NIH-sponsored trial reported fewer preterm deliveries [3], which led to FDA approval of Makena in 2011 [2]. The later PROLONG trial did not show the same benefit [4][5], and the FDA withdrew approval in April 2023 [2].
infobox: Prescription-only; Makena approval withdrawn in the US in 2023 [2]

paras: Gynecologic uses listed for the product include advanced uterine adenocarcinoma, amenorrhea, abnormal uterine bleeding due to hormonal imbalance, and as a test of endogenous estrogen production [6]. Other uses described include premenstrual syndrome, threatened miscarriage, menopausal hormone therapy and feminizing hormone therapy [2].
The obstetric use is reduction of recurrent preterm birth in singleton pregnancies with a history of spontaneous preterm birth, typically as a weekly injection in the second and third trimesters [7].

A 2003 double-blind trial in women with a prior spontaneous preterm delivery found that weekly 17P reduced the risk of delivery before 37 weeks compared with placebo [3]. A 1975 study had also reported efficacy against premature labor [8], and a 1957 JAMA item discussed the drug [9].

A trial in twin pregnancies did not find a benefit [10]. The larger PROLONG trial, a multicenter international randomized double-blind trial, was designed to confirm the earlier result [4]. Reviews note that neither PROLONG nor the OPPTIMUM trial of vaginal progesterone demonstrated efficacy, and that there is little long-term follow-up data [5]. An individual participant data meta-analysis (EPPPIC) and a network meta-analysis compared progestogens and other interventions for preterm birth prevention [11][12]. A 2023 review states that 17-OHPC may reduce recurrent preterm birth in singletons while vaginal progesterone has support in selected high-risk pregnancies [7].

Injection-site reactions are the most commonly reported effect, with pain in about 35 percent and swelling in about 17 percent of users in one summary; urticaria, itching and nausea are also reported [2]. The US label for the non-pregnancy product lists thromboembolic events including pulmonary embolism and stroke reported with progestins, neuro-ocular lesions, edema, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness, weight changes and headache, and notes that progestins may reduce glucose tolerance [6].

17-OHPC is a progesterone derivative whose caproate (hexanoate) ester prolongs its action after oil-based intramuscular injection [1][2]. Reported half-life is about 7.8 days in non-pregnant women, about 16-17 days in singleton pregnancy and about 10 days in twin pregnancy [2].

Developed at Schering in 1953 and reported in 1954, it was marketed in Japan from about 1954-55 and in the US as Delalutin in 1956 [2]. A 1957 JAMA item on the drug shows it was in clinical discussion by then [9]. Squibb voluntarily withdrew Delalutin in 1999; after the 2003 trial, the FDA approved Makena in February 2011 as an orphan drug. Covis Pharma agreed to withdraw it in March 2023 and the FDA withdrew approval in April 2023; in 2024 an EU committee recommended suspending marketing authorizations [2].

Hydroxyprogesterone caproate is discussed mainly in medical and hormone-therapy settings rather than in looksmaxxing forums. Combination products with estradiol esters have been sold under names such as Gravibinon and Primosiston in some countries [2].
